Ostomy Canada Society runs chapters and peer support groups across the country, searchable by distance from where you live
Their Visitor Program trains people who have an ostomy to talk with people who have just had one — lived experience, not clinical advice
If you are between roughly 20 and 40, ask about Gutsy Gang social clubs — they run in Vancouver, Calgary, Saskatoon, Winnipeg, Hamilton, Toronto, and Niagara
A peer visitor is not a substitute for your NSWOC. Most people find they want both.
Peer support is its own kind of care
chapters.everyday-liivving.categories.10: Pack your supplies in your carry-on. CATSA permits ostomy supplies in both carry-on and checked baggage, so split them — enough in the carry-on to cover the whole journey and a delay, and a backup set in the checked bag. Never let the only set be the one in the hold
Take roughly twice what you expect to need for the trip

Cut your barriers to size before you leave, so they are ready if you need to change on the plane. Scissors are not the reason — in Canada, blades of 6 cm or less are allowed in carry-on. Pre-cutting simply spares you cutting a barrier on a tray table, and scissors rules are tighter in some other countries
CATSA permits ostomy supplies in both carry-on and checked baggage, so you should not be turned back for carrying them — though the final decision on any item rests with the screening officer

Being medical supplies is not a blanket exemption from the liquids rule. That exemption covers prescription and essential non-prescription medication, and CATSA states that ostomy paste tubes must be 100 mL or less and travel in your clear 1 L bag. Treat adhesive remover, barrier spray and lubricating deodorant the same way, or pack full sizes in checked baggage

You can ask for privacy. CATSA says you can request a private screening room, and if a physical search or a swab is needed you can ask for that to be done there. It helps to tell the officer you have an ostomy pouch, and roughly where it is, before screening starts

Ostomy Canada publishes a printable Traveller’s Communication Card, and Coloplast Care offers a travel certificate to people enrolled in its program. Convatec’s card is written for US screening and its travel pass is a UK document, so check which version you are getting. None of these is an official pass and CATSA does not require documentation — the card simply saves explaining

Screening rules change and vary by country. Check CATSA’s current guidance before you fly, and note that it covers flights leaving Canada — for the return leg, check the rules where you are flying out of. What CATSA allows in your carry-on leaving Toronto is not a guarantee coming back.

Cabin pressure falls in flight, so gas already in the pouch expands a little. In practice the effect is small and a filtered pouch vents most of it — Ostomy Canada is explicit that the pouch will not blow up
If your pouch does balloon on a flight, the cause is usually swallowed air, fizzy drinks, gassy food, or sitting still for hours. Vent or empty it and carry on
Empty before boarding and again during the flight rather than waiting for it to feel necessary. An aisle seat makes that discreet rather than an event
chapters.everyday-liivving.categories.11: Adhesive works less well when it is cold. A barrier that has been in a cold car or an unheated porch will not bond as readily

Warm the barrier before applying — hold it between your palms for a minute, or tuck it under your clothing against your body — then press it in place for a full minute or two. Use body heat only: not a hairdryer, radiator or microwave. Too much heat damages the adhesive, and because the stoma has no nerve endings it cannot warn you when something is too hot
If your wear time drops every winter, start with the temperature of your supplies rather than your skin — a barrier stored or carried cold is the more likely explanation

Store spare supplies somewhere room temperature — Ostomy Canada suggests roughly 15 to 30°C — rather than a garage, shed, or the trunk of a car. Coloplast’s instructions for use state the product must not be stored under freezing conditions. Heat is a problem too, so those same spots are worth avoiding in July as much as in January.
Winter, and why things stop sticking
chapters.everyday-liivving.categories.12: Find out where the nearest pharmacy is and how long it would take to reach — but treat it as a backup, not a plan. Pharmacies carry a limited range and are unlikely to stock your exact barrier and pouch
Take at least double what you need. There is no version of this trip where running out is a minor inconvenience

Plan disposal, and keep the contents and the pouch separate in your head. Contents go into a toilet where there is one; in the backcountry treat them as any human waste — a cathole 15 to 20 cm deep, at least 60 m from water, trails and camp, or packed out where that is the rule. The pouch itself never goes down a toilet: it blocks the line, and a septic system or holding tank is far less forgiving than a municipal one

If you irrigate, think it through carefully before committing to somewhere without running water. A routine needs roughly 500 to 1,000 mL of lukewarm water clean enough to drink, about an hour at a toilet, and somewhere for the output to go — and it repeats every day or two. Cold water causes cramping, which is harder to manage away from a tap. If you would not drink the water, do not irrigate with it.
chapters.everyday-liivving.categories.13: Your entitlement is set by the province you live in — you qualify through your provincial coverage, not through the store. That does not mean you can buy anywhere
Ontario and Quebec pay a set amount and leave the choice of retailer to you. Saskatchewan will reimburse products bought in another province if you send a paid receipt showing what you purchased

Alberta works differently: AADL requires you to buy from an approved Alberta vendor, does not fund online-only shops, and does not reimburse people who buy on their own. In Manitoba you do not buy at all — supplies are ordered through the provincial program and shipped from Winnipeg. In British Columbia, anything ordered online has to come from a PharmaCare-authorized provider

Check your own program’s vendor rules before you order from out of province — including from us. Moving provinces is a different situation entirely and resets your coverage; that is in Funding & Coverage.
chapters.everyday-liivving.categories.14: Supply exchanges exist, including Facebook groups such as Ostomy Supplies Exchange Canada, and some people do find what they need this way. Ostomy Canada also advises caution: a barrier that suited someone else’s stoma, or one stored badly, can leak or damage your skin

Check the expiry date, that packaging is intact and unopened, and that the size matches what you use. Ask how the supplies were stored too — heat and damp shorten the life of an adhesive barrier well before its printed expiry

Do not accept anything whose inner packaging has been opened. Most pouches and barriers are supplied non-sterile, so the reason is less about sterility than the adhesive: once the seal is broken you cannot tell how long it has been exposed to air

Local chapters and support groups often take in surplus supplies and pass them to members who need them. Friends of Ostomates Worldwide Canada also collects surplus, but ships it to partner organizations overseas rather than to individuals here — it states it cannot support individual requests. If you are donating, it asks that items stay in their packaging.
chapters.everyday-liivving.categories.15: There is no national ostomy program. The amount, the model, and who approves it all change at the provincial border
Moving provinces resets everything — including which forms you file and who has to sign them

Who signs off changes at the border: a physician or nurse practitioner in Ontario and Nova Scotia, nobody clinical in Quebec or British Columbia, and a registered nurse — usually an NSWOC — in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Saskatchewan will not accept a self-application at all
We have checked every province and territory against its own government page — see Funding & Coverage for what yours pays, who has to sign off, and the dates that catch people out.
What coverage actually looks like in Canada
chapters.everyday-liivving.categories.16: All three major manufacturers run free support programs — samples, phone lines, and access to ostomy nurses
You do not have to buy from us, or from them, to use these
They will also help you work out what your province covers, which is often the fastest way to get an answer
chapters.everyday-liivving.categories.17: World Ostomy Day runs every three years, not every year — the last was 4 October 2025, and the next falls in 2028
In the years between, Canada still marks the first Saturday of October, anchored by Ostomy Canada’s Step Up for Ostomy campaign
Chapters usually run local events — the chapter finder is the fastest way to see what is happening near you
chapters.everyday-liivving.categories.18: Reading someone describe their first month is worth more than any checklist we could write
We are collecting stories from Canadians with ostomies — surgery, work, travel, dating, sport, all of it
If you would like to share yours, tell the care team and we will be in touch about how it works
Stories from people who have one
Food is broken down in the stomach and small intestine, and that part is usually unchanged — this is why you still absorb your nutrition
The colon’s main job is reclaiming water and salt from what is left, and forming stool. A colostomy leaves most of that intact; an ileostomy bypasses it almost entirely

A urostomy does not change how food is digested — it diverts urine before the kidneys reach the bladder, so most of the food questions here are not yours. Fluid is the opposite: you need more of it than before, steadily through the day, because a well-flushed system is what protects against infection and stones. Ask your urologist or NSWOC what daily target fits you
This is the single most useful thing to understand: an ileostomy is not "a colostomy higher up". The missing colon is why output is looser, why fluid and salt matter more, and why the advice differs.
Most teams suggest a lower-fibre period straight after surgery. It is temporary, and it is about swelling at the stoma rather than about fibre being bad for you
Your stoma is swollen at first and shrinks over the following weeks, so the opening it can pass comfortably gets bigger too
Appetite is often poor early on. Small, frequent meals tend to sit better than three large ones
How long this lasts is your surgical team’s call, not a fixed rule — it varies by surgery and by person. Ask when you should be moving on rather than assuming.
One new food at a time, in a small amount, with a couple of days before the next one — otherwise you cannot tell what caused what
Chew far more than feels necessary. With an ileostomy especially, chewing is doing work your colon used to do
Keep a rough note for a few weeks. Patterns show up quickly and then you can stop writing things down

Tolerance is genuinely individual. Two people with the same surgery often land on completely different lists, so treat anyone else’s "foods to avoid" list — including one you find online — as a starting hypothesis rather than a rule.
Commonly reported as harder to pass
Fibrous or stringy foods — celery, corn, mushrooms, coconut, pineapple, dried fruit
Skins, pips and casings — apple peel, sweetcorn, nuts, popcorn, sausage skins
How to approach them rather than avoid them forever
Cut small, cook well, chew thoroughly, and try a small amount on a day when you are not out
Plenty of people go back to all of these. The point is caution, not a permanent ban
If you have an ileostomy and have had a blockage before, talk to your NSWOC or a dietitian before reintroducing this group. That is a different conversation from a first attempt.
Foods people often find need care
With an ileostomy you lose more water and more sodium than you did before, and you lose it steadily rather than noticeably
Thirst is a late signal. Darker urine, headache, cramps, and feeling flat often arrive first
Plain water alone can sometimes make high output worse — an oral rehydration solution replaces salt as well as fluid
Ask your NSWOC or pharmacist what to keep at home before you need it. Rehydration solutions are cheap, keep well, and are far more useful bought in advance than at 2am.
Gas usually settles over the first months as your gut adapts — early gas is not a sign of how things will stay
Swallowed air is a bigger contributor than most people expect: eating quickly, straws, chewing gum, fizzy drinks
Filters wet out and stop working. That is the filter doing its job and reaching the end of it, not a defect
Starchy foods — white rice, pasta, bread, potato without skin, banana, smooth peanut butter, marshmallows
Very sugary drinks, alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, and large amounts of fruit

These are patterns many people notice, not instructions. If you are using food to manage persistent high output rather than an occasional day, that needs an NSWOC or dietitian rather than a longer list of foods.
Extended-release, slow-release and enteric-coated tablets are designed to dissolve over a long stretch of gut — with an ileostomy they can pass straight through, intact and unabsorbed
People sometimes see whole tablets in the pouch. That is worth reporting rather than ignoring
This can quietly affect anything that matters — blood pressure, thyroid, mental health medication, contraception
Bring your full medication list to a pharmacist and say you have an ileostomy. There is often an immediate-release or liquid alternative. Do not stop or change anything yourself.
chapters.everyday-liivving.categoriesInt: Two halves. The first is your own body settling into a routine — what you eat, what comes out, and what changes. The second is everything around it: the money, the travel, and the help that exists in Canada but is almost never in one place. Most of that half links out, because those organizations do it better than we could.
You are not doing this alone
What exists, and who it is for
chapters.everyday-liivving.closing.body: Most of this stops being a question within a few months. The part that does not — the money, and finding people who have one — is the part most people never find out about, which is the only reason this page needed writing.
chapters.everyday-liivving.focus: Adding foods back and what to watch for, fluid and salt, gas and odour, the medication question, and then the practical Canadian ones — flying, winter adhesion, going remote, ordering across provincial lines, what coverage actually looks like province by province, and how to find people near you.
chapters.everyday-liivving.governance.di: This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for assessment by your NSWOC, surgeon, or physician. Fit, skin, and product choices depend on your body and your surgery — talk to your care team before changing anything.
chapters.everyday-liivving.heroBody: Eating again, and everything around the edges of a day — travel, winter, money, and the people and programs that exist in Canada.
chapters.everyday-liivving.pharmacist.bo: Product fit, restock questions, and everyday concerns — chat with an Ontario pharmacist during business hours (until 5 p.m. Eastern). Olivia helps with shopping anytime; she does not give medical advice.
chapters.everyday-liivving.pharmacist.he: Fit questions that do not need a waiting room
Ontario and Quebec send a set amount each year and you buy your own supplies. If you use more than the grant covers, the overage is yours — and may be claimable as a medical expense.
A flat grant, paid to you
British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Newfoundland cover a share and you pay the rest, often up to an annual cap. Low income can reduce your share to nothing.
Manitoba does not reimburse — the program sends the supplies. You are registered through an NSWOC after surgery rather than applying yourself.
PEI is income-tiered. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick route by category — seniors, social assistance, or specific programs — so there is no general coverage to apply for.
Four ways provinces pay — knowing yours saves you money
chapters.everyday-liivving.resources.1.b: These are run by patient organizations and specialist nurses, not by us. They are free, and they are better at this than any retailer.
chapters.everyday-liivving.resources.1.h: Support that is already out there
chapters.everyday-liivving.resources.1.l: Search by distance from your postal code, from 10 km out to 500 km. Also lists Gutsy Gang social clubs for younger adults.
Find a chapter or peer support group
Trained peer visitors who have an ostomy themselves. Requested through your local chapter, usually after a referral from your surgeon or NSWOC.
Nurses Specialized in Wound, Ostomy and Continence — the clinical specialists for stoma care in Canada. Many hospitals have one; some see outpatients for life.
A week at Camp Horizon in Bragg Creek, Alberta, for kids and teens with ostomies. Partial and full funding is available — ask, do not assume the fee is the barrier.
chapters.everyday-liivving.resources.2.b: All three are free and none of them require you to buy from us. We have listed what each program offers — not whose products are better, which is not our call to make.
chapters.everyday-liivving.resources.2.l: Free personalized support regardless of which brand you use, including help navigating coverage. Canadian line: 1-800-263-7421.
Ongoing educational support, phone access, samples, and the MyOstomy app for tracking changes and output. Consumer support: 1-866-293-6349.
Staged around the journey — before surgery, right after, and living with one. Includes video appointments with a certified ostomy nurse. 1-800-465-6302.
chapters.everyday-liivving.resources.3.b: Amounts and rules change, and they change by province. Always confirm against the official source before you plan around a number.
chapters.everyday-liivving.resources.3.l: The best public summary of what each province and territory covers, with links through to the official program pages.

Applied for under the “eliminating” category, but having an ostomy does not qualify you on its own — the funding section walks through the test the CRA actually applies. Approval can unlock the RDSP and other credits, so it is worth reading before you start the paperwork.
Full coverage with no annual cap for registered First Nations and recognized Inuit. This replaces the provincial route rather than topping it up.
chapters.everyday-liivving.resources.4.b: Written by nurses and patient organizations, free, and more thorough than anything on this page.
chapters.everyday-liivving.resources.4.l: Clinician-written patient guides, one per ostomy type, including the less commonly covered ones — jejunostomy, gastrostomy, and gastro-jejunostomy.
Living with an ileostomy, colostomy, or ileal conduit
American, so the funding sections will not apply here — but the clinical and practical content is excellent and freely available.
The national awareness and fundraising campaign that anchors the first Saturday of October in Canada.

chapters.get-to-know-your-stoma.categori: Colostomy, ileostomy, and urostomy each shape output and daily care a little differently
A stoma can be temporary or permanent — your care team decides with you
Healthy peristomal skin should look like the skin on the other side of your abdomen
Stoma Basics
What tends to suit a one-piece
You want the lowest profile under clothes, and the simplest routine
Your skin is settled and you are not changing the pouch more often than the barrier
What tends to suit a two-piece
You empty or swap pouches often and would rather not disturb the barrier each time
You want to alternate between a closed pouch for going out and a drainable one at home
Reaching or dexterity is difficult, and doing the two steps separately is easier
Neither is better. Plenty of people use both — a two-piece for workdays and a one-piece for swimming, for instance.
One-piece or two-piece
A flat barrier suits a stoma that protrudes onto reasonably even skin, which is most people
Convexity curves toward your skin to help a flat or retracted stoma stand out, or to smooth a dip or crease that output keeps tracking into
It comes in soft and firm versions and different depths, and the right one depends on your abdomen, your stoma, and how your skin behaves under pressure

This is the one product decision on the whole site that we would rather you did not make alone. Convexity applied to the wrong abdomen can cause a pressure injury, and it is a common reason people end up with skin damage they did not have before. Ask your NSWOC to assess you — most will let you try one before you buy a box.
Flat or convex — please ask before you switch
For sealing and skin
Barrier rings and seals — mouldable, they fill small dips and add a little protection right at the stoma edge
Paste — not glue. It is a filler for creases and uneven skin. Most contain alcohol, so it can sting on broken skin
Stoma powder — for weepy, broken skin only, dusted on and the excess brushed off. It does not belong under an intact barrier on healthy skin
Barrier film or wipes — a thin protective layer between adhesive and skin, useful if removal is irritating your skin
For comfort and confidence
Adhesive remover — reduces the pulling on your skin at removal, which matters more the more often you change
Belts — add security and are sometimes recommended alongside convexity. They need sizing
Lubricating deodorant — helps output drop to the bottom of the pouch and controls odour, which also helps with pancaking

What none of them do is rescue a barrier that is the wrong size or the wrong shape for you. If you are reaching for two or three accessories to make one system stay on, the system is the problem — that is a fit review, not a shopping list.
What accessories actually do
Hollister, Coloplast and Convatec all send free samples in Canada, whether or not you buy from them, and regardless of which brand you currently use
Ask for a sample of anything you are considering switching to — barriers, rings, convex products, belts
Give a new product a few changes before deciding. First impressions are often about unfamiliarity rather than fit
Their contact details are in Everyday Liivving. There is no obligation attached, and it is a much cheaper way to find what works than buying full boxes.
Try it before you buy a box
Leaks that have started happening when they were not before
Weight change in either direction, which alters the shape of the area around your stoma
A new bulge, or the skin around the stoma changing shape
Skin that is not fully healed by the next change
Pregnancy, or any further abdominal surgery
A fit review is a normal part of ostomy care, not an admission that something has gone wrong. Bodies change, and the system that suited you last year may simply not be the right one now.
When to ask for a fit review
What often helps
Re-measure. Stoma size changes for months after surgery, and an opening cut to last month’s size is one of the most common causes of a leak
Check where the leak starts — from under the barrier, or from the edge. They point at different problems
Make sure skin is completely dry before the barrier goes on, and hold it in place so body heat can set the seal
When to call your NSWOC
Leaks more than occasionally, or a pattern you cannot explain
Skin that has not fully healed between changes

Repeated leaking usually means the fit is wrong, not that you are doing it wrong. Convexity, rings and pastes can all help — but which one depends on your abdomen and your stoma, so that is an assessment rather than a shopping decision. The wrong convexity can cause a pressure injury.
Leaks and short wear time
What is happening
The pouch film sticks to itself, so output cannot drop away from the stoma and pushes up under the barrier instead
It is more common with thicker output and with filters that pull the air out quickly
What often helps
A puff of air in the pouch before you close it
A lubricating deodorant, which helps output slide to the bottom
If it is constant, or your output has become noticeably thicker than it used to be, mention it — that is worth looking at rather than working around.
Pancaking
What often helps
Filters do wet out and stop working — that is normal rather than a fault
Gas patterns often settle over the first months as your gut adjusts
Eating and drinking more slowly means swallowing less air
When to call your NSWOC
A sudden change in gas alongside pain, or output that stops
Food affects gas differently for everyone, and post-surgery advice differs by ostomy type — so this is a conversation with your team or a dietitian rather than a list to follow.
Ballooning and gas
Please do not self-diagnose this one
Irritation from output, a fungal rash, a contact allergy, and a few less common conditions look almost identical to the eye
They have opposite treatments — the wrong one makes several of them worse
What is safe to do meanwhile
Keep the area clean with warm water only — no oils, lotions, or fragranced products under the barrier
Check the opening is not cut larger than the stoma, which leaves skin exposed to output
Photograph it before your appointment, since skin changes between changes
Any skin that is broken, weeping, bleeding, or still not healed by the next change needs an NSWOC to look at it — not a product recommendation from the internet.
Sore, itchy, or weeping skin
Why it matters more with an ileostomy
An ileostomy puts out more fluid and more salt, so dehydration builds faster and less obviously than people expect
Thirst is not a reliable early sign — dark urine, headache, and feeling washed out often come first
When to call
A sustained jump in output lasting more than a day
Watery, high-volume output that is not settling
Feeling dizzy, confused, or unusually weak alongside it
High output is the leading reason people are readmitted after ostomy surgery. It is worth phoning about early rather than waiting to see.
Output that changes
NSWOCC publishes free patient guides for several of these, including jejunostomy and gastrostomy, in English and French. They are linked from Everyday Liivving.
Other stomas you may hear about
Jejunostomy — formed higher in the small bowel than an ileostomy. Output is greater and more watery, and fluid, salt and nutrition need closer specialist follow-up
Ileal conduit — the most common form of urostomy, where urine is diverted through a short piece of bowel to a stoma

Nephrostomy — a tube that drains urine straight from the kidney. It comes out through the skin of your back rather than through a stoma on the abdomen, and drains into a bag usually strapped to your thigh under your clothes. It is often temporary
Continent diversions, which work differently

An ileoanal pouch (often called a J-pouch) is designed to leave you with no stoma in the long run — an internal reservoir is joined to the anus, so you pass stool the usual way. It normally takes two or three operations, and most people have a temporary ileostomy for a few months in between. Once it is working, stool is looser and you go more often, commonly five to ten times a day, settling with time

A continent ileostomy, such as a Kock pouch, has a small flush stoma and an internal reservoir made from small bowel. There is no pouch to wear — you drain it with a catheter, usually two to four times a day, and cover the stoma with a cap or gauze in between

A Mitrofanoff is a different operation, for urine rather than stool. A narrow channel, usually made from the appendix, runs from your own bladder to a small stoma, and you pass a catheter through it to empty

Continent diversions are cared for quite differently from a conventional stoma. Advice about pouches, barriers and flanges will not apply to you — advice about diet, fluids and salt still does. Two things this site does not cover. With a bowel reservoir such as a Kock pouch, if the catheter will not pass, stop rather than persisting, rest an hour and try again, and get advice that day if you still cannot drain. With a Mitrofanoff, which drains urine, do not keep trying — an unemptied bladder needs an emergency department the same day. Your surgical team and NSWOC are the right source for both.
The less common diversions
What it usually is
A parastomal hernia — the abdominal wall weakening around the stoma. It is common and it is not something you caused
It often changes how your barrier sits, so leaks can start at the same time
When to call your NSWOC
Any new bulge, or a change in the shape of the area around your stoma
Support garments help many people, but they have to be sized and chosen for the specific hernia — buying one without an assessment can make the fit worse rather than better.
A bulge around the stoma
High-waisted styles and soft layers can keep a pouch secure and low-profile
Support belts or wraps for active days when you want extra hold
You do not have to hide your pouch — comfort and preference come first
Clothing & Confidence
Empty when the pouch is about one-third to one-half full to reduce leak risk
Pack supplies in your carry-on — never only in checked bags
Plan bathroom stops the way you plan coffee: early and without apology
Travel & Workdays
Talk about what helps you feel secure — timing, clothing, or a support wrap
Confidence grows with a routine that has already worked at home
Your pace is the right pace
Intimacy & Social Ease
Many people prefer morning changes when output is often lower
Lay out supplies like a station before you start
Restock before you run low — clockwork beats last-minute stress
Rest & Routine

A parastomal hernia is a bulge beside the stoma, where the abdominal wall has weakened and what is underneath pushes through. It is common, and more likely the longer you have a stoma. Ordinary daily life does not cause it, though not smoking, keeping to a healthy weight and avoiding straining all lower the risk

Follow the lifting advice your surgical team gives you, and ask them to show you how to lift rather than only what to avoid. Your abdominal wall is still healing in the early weeks, so build up gradually — technique matters more than a fixed weight limit

Gentle core and breathing exercises usually start within the first few days, and you build from there. What is right for you depends on your fitness as much as your surgery — a physiotherapist can set the pace with you

Many people find a support garment comfortable and reassuring, particularly if a hernia is already there. It is worth knowing that support wear has not been shown to prevent a hernia — it is for comfort and confidence. If you have one, ask your NSWOC to measure and fit you, since a garment that is too tight can restrict your movement and breathing.
Hernias, lifting and your core
Walking usually comes first and starts early. Everything beyond that is a conversation about timing with your surgical team

Swimming is fine once your wounds are fully healed — your pouch is water-resistant and, fitted well, designed not to leak. Change it well before you swim rather than just beforehand so the adhesive can settle, and cover the filter with the sticker provided

Contact sports are worth raising, since a stoma guard protects against a direct blow. Heavy lifting is a separate question — a guard does not help there. Technique, breathing out on the effort and building up gradually do, and most people get back to what they did before
Ostomy Canada and the manufacturer support programs both run activity resources, and plenty of ostomates return to running, swimming, weights, and team sport.
Getting back to activity
Your equipment
Appliance or pouching system — the whole setup: the barrier plus the pouch

Barrier, wafer or baseplate — the part that sticks to your skin. Many people say flange for this too, but on some two-piece systems flange means the plastic ring that clicks the pouch on. If you are ordering, check which one your brand means

Convexity — a barrier that curves outward towards your skin instead of lying flat, to help a flat or retracted stoma stand out or to smooth a crease. It comes in soft and firm versions and different depths. Helpful for some abdomens, harmful for others, so it is an assessment rather than a purchase
Your body
Peristomal skin — the skin around the stoma. It starts where the stoma meets your skin and takes in everything your barrier, tape or belt touches
Output — what comes out of the stoma. You will hear it used far more often than you might expect
Mucocutaneous junction — where the stoma meets your skin
Your people
NSWOC — Nurse Specialized in Wound, Ostomy and Continence. The Canadian specialist for stoma care, and the term used nationally
ET nurse or enterostomal therapy nurse — the older term for the same role. It still appears in official documents, including Saskatchewan’s SAIL program rules
WOCN Society — the American organization, which you will meet in US-published material. There the nurse is a WOC nurse, and a certified one is a CWOCN
Words you will hear
One-piece: barrier and pouch are joined — simple and low-profile
Two-piece: barrier stays while you change pouches — flexible for frequent emptying
Your NSWOC or pharmacist can help you find what seals best for your body
One-Piece vs Two-Piece
Clean with warm water; avoid oils, fragrances, and lotion under the barrier
Pat dry completely — dry skin seals better than damp skin
Powder, paste, rings, and wipes are tools for seal and comfort — add only what you need
Skin Comfort
Empty drainable pouches at about one-third to one-half full
Closed pouches are replaced as needed through the day
Full system changes are often every few days — or sooner if you feel burning, itching, or a leak
Output & Patterns
Measure during the first months — stoma size can change as swelling settles
An opening that is too large exposes skin; too small can injure the stoma
Aim for a close fit around the stoma edge so output lands in the pouch, not on skin
Fit Changes
Persistent leaks, redness, pain, or skin that will not heal
Sudden changes in output, swelling, or how your barrier wears
Your NSWOC is the clinical guide; Ontario pharmacists can help with everyday product questions in chat
When to Ask
Use the measuring guide that comes in the box — hold it over the stoma and pick the closest shape and size
Cut so the opening sits close to the edge of the stoma. Too large exposes skin to output; too small can rub or injure the stoma
Not all stomas are round. Many are oval, and a cut-to-fit barrier can be shaped to match

Re-measure regularly for the first few months, and again after any weight change or a hernia. A barrier cut to a size from two months ago is one of the most common reasons a system that used to work suddenly does not.
Measure before you order
A pouching system is a skin barrier (wafer/flange) plus a pouch. Fit and skin health drive comfort more than anything else.
Understanding without overwhelm
Know your setup
Knowing your stoma is not a test — it is a quieter relationship with fit, skin, and the products that earn their place on your shelf.
Comfort is a skill you build

chapters.get-to-know-your-stoma.heroBody: Clear, kind education about your stoma — how it works, what changes, and what to do when something is not right.
chapters.get-to-know-your-stoma.pharmaci: Not sure if you need convex, a ring, or a different wipe? Chat with an Ontario pharmacist during business hours — until 5 p.m. Eastern. For clinical stoma concerns, your NSWOC remains your primary resource.
chapters.get-to-know-your-stoma.title: Your Stoma, and Your Fit
chapters.get-to-know-your-stoma.urgent.a: Go to your nearest emergency department or call 911. Do not wait for a callback, and do not troubleshoot a dusky stoma at home.
chapters.get-to-know-your-stoma.urgent.h: Some things are not a website question
chapters.get-to-know-your-stoma.urgent.i: Most stoma worries can wait for your next NSWOC appointment. These cannot. Seek urgent medical care if you notice:
chapters.get-to-know-your-stoma.urgent.s: A stoma that turns dark, dusky, purple, or feels cold to the touch
Severe abdominal pain, or vomiting with no output for several hours — this can mean a blockage
Heavy or continuous bleeding from the stoma itself, not just a spot from cleaning
Fever, or skin around the stoma that is hot, spreading red, and painful
Confusion, severe dizziness, or very dark urine alongside high output — signs of significant dehydration
A catheter that will not pass, if you empty a continent diversion or a Mitrofanoff that way — a reservoir that cannot be drained will not wait
chapters.get-to-know-your-stoma.vibe: Clear, kind, and demystifying — education without overwhelm.

Tell your doctor
If it is not easing, or you are struggling to get through the day
Ostomy Canada peer visitor
Ask your surgeon or NSWOC for a referral, or contact your local chapter yourself.
If you want to talk to someone who has been through it
Feeling frightened, angry, or numb is an ordinary reaction to this news, not a sign you are handling it badly
The waiting is hard, and recovery has its own hard parts — learning the routine takes most people months rather than weeks

People with ostomies work, travel, swim, date, have children, and play sport. That is the ordinary outcome, not the exceptional one — most of it comes back once you have healed, which usually takes months rather than weeks

It does get easier. If it is not easing, or you are struggling to get through the day, tell your NSWOC or doctor rather than waiting it out — low mood after this surgery is common and treatable. If you want to talk to someone who has been through it, Ostomy Canada trains peer visitors: ask your surgeon or NSWOC for a referral, or contact your local chapter yourself. See Everyday Liivving.

chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.2: by an NSWOC or your surgeon
your surgeon makes the final call
Checked while you sit, stand, and bend
And other things your NSWOC checks

Siting means an NSWOC or your surgeon marks the best spot on your abdomen before your operation, while you are awake. Your surgeon makes the final call during surgery, so sometimes more than one spot is marked
They check the spot while you sit, stand, and bend, and keep it clear of your waistband, skin folds, scars, and your beltline

Placement affects how well every appliance you ever wear will seal, and people marked before surgery tend to have fewer leaks. If leaks do happen they are usually fixable with a different appliance or an added seal, whatever the shape of your abdomen

This is the thing people most often do not know to ask for, and it is much harder to fix afterwards. If nobody has mentioned siting, ask. That includes emergency surgery — Canadian guidance says emergency patients should still be marked before the anesthetic wherever possible, and it matters more then, not less.
Ask for stoma siting — this one matters most
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.3: Which type of ostomy, and is it expected to be permanent or reversible? If reversible, roughly when might that be considered?
Will I be seen by an NSWOC before surgery for siting, and who will teach me afterwards?
What will my output be like, and what should I expect in the first weeks?
Who do I contact when I get home, and what counts as urgent?
Write them down and take the list in. It is completely normal to forget every question the moment someone in scrubs walks in.
Questions worth asking before you go in
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.4: Loose, high-waisted clothing for going home — nothing that sits across where the stoma will be
Your usual medications list, which the ward will want anyway and which matters later for absorption
Arrange help for the first week or two if you can. Lifting is restricted afterwards, and that includes shopping and laundry
What to pack, and what to arrange
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.5: You do not need to learn the pouch change unless they want you to — many people prefer to keep that private, and that is worth asking rather than assuming
Practical help lands better than reassurance early on: driving, cooking, and taking over the lifting they are not allowed to do
Your own reaction is allowed to be complicated. Peer support groups usually welcome partners and family too
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.6: Fatigue is normal — rest is part of recovery
Your care team will send you home with a starter setup; learning takes practice, not perfection
Many people feel more confident within four to eight weeks
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.7: Gather supplies first: new system, measuring guide, scissors if needed, warm water, soft cloth, disposal bag
Remove gently — never rip; wet a cloth to help release adhesive if needed
Clean, dry, measure, apply, and hold the barrier so body heat activates the seal
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.8: Pouches and barriers that match your system (one-piece or two-piece)
Skin protectant wipe, powder if recommended, disposal bags
A go-bag for outings from day one
Try The Fresh Start kit — customize quantities before checkout.

Adhesive remover and skin protectant if you use them
A spare underwear or liner for peace of mind away from home

Chapter 02 — Some things are not a website question
chapters.new-to-the-journey.vibe: Supportive and demystifying — a soft place to land.
Pediatric ostomy care belongs with a children’s hospital team — the service that created the stoma, working with a nurse who practises in pediatrics. One practical note: “pediatric NSWOC” describes where a nurse works rather than a credential you can search for, and the NSWOCC directory filters by city and by wound, ostomy or continence, with no pediatric option. So the hospital team is the first call, and the one who can point you to the right nurse near you. Coverage for children differs from the adult rules — see Funding & Coverage.

A small body has very little fluid in reserve, so a child — especially a baby with an ileostomy — can get dehydrated far faster than an adult losing the same amount. Steady salt loss can also show up as poor weight gain long before anything looks like dehydration, which is why your team may weigh your baby often

Ask what your child’s normal output is and what counts as too much for their size. Call the same day for output that suddenly rises or turns watery, fewer wet diapers, no tears, a sunken soft spot, unusual sleepiness, or weight that stalls or drops — that is a call to your team, not something to manage with extra fluids at home
A child’s stoma is not a smaller version of an adult one. They grow, so sizes change constantly — re-measuring is routine rather than occasional

Pediatric products are a real category rather than repackaged adult stock, shaped smaller and more flexibly for a small abdomen. The adhesive is the part that gets overstated: it is largely the same material as the adult ranges. A baby born at term starts with skin barrier function much like an adult’s, so the extra caution about fragile skin is really for babies born early or at low birth weight, and children who are unwell

When a pouch keeps lifting, the answer is usually to change it more often rather than to make it stick harder — pediatric barriers are thinner, so they hold up to output for less time. Adhesive removers, barrier films, skin cement and benzoin are generally avoided in infants and young children, because more of any chemical is absorbed through their skin and a stronger bond can tear it on removal. A seal that keeps failing is a call to your child’s ostomy nurse, not a trip for stronger products
Two things worth knowing before they happen

A child’s stoma can prolapse — telescope outward and look alarmingly long. It is more common in children than in adults and usually not an emergency, but colour matters more than length: call urgently if it darkens or goes dusky, if your child is in pain, or if output stops
In a child with an ileostomy, high-fibre foods can cause a blockage, so new foods go in one at a time. Ask your team what each of these looks like for your child, and which number to call after hours

School needs a written plan rather than a conversation in September: who knows and who backs them up on days they are away, where a spare kit and a full change of clothes live, private washroom access without having to ask in front of the class, and a number the school can call

Most Canadian schools have no nurse on site, so ask who owns the plan — usually the principal, sometimes a public health nurse — and make sure supply teachers get it. Most schools have never been asked before, so expect to be the one explaining

Ask the children’s hospital about transition planning a year or two before it happens, and about who the adult service will be. The handoff around seventeen or eighteen is the point at which families most often fall out of specialist care altogether, and it goes better when it is arranged rather than arrived at
Children, and the people raising them
There is no rule about when to tell a partner, and no version of it you owe anyone. Some people say it early so it is out of the way; others wait until someone knows them a bit first
It often goes fine. It sometimes does not — and if someone decides they cannot be with you because of your stoma, that is information about them rather than a sign you handled it wrong
Practise it once out loud, with a friend or a peer visitor, before it matters. It is easier the second time

University accommodations are real and not a favour, but they usually run through two offices: exam arrangements through accessibility services, residence through campus housing, on a separate application. Both want documentation from your care team and both have deadlines that can fall months before term, so ask early — and what is on offer varies, since a private washroom is not something every campus provides

Alcohol changes output for a lot of people, but the bigger issue is fluid. It is a diuretic, and with an ileostomy you are already losing more water and salt than you used to — dehydration is the most common reason people end up back in hospital after ileostomy surgery. A long night out is still worth planning around rather than avoiding, and if your output is already high, ask your NSWOC or dietitian what your fluid plan should look like first

Ostomy Canada runs Gutsy Gang social clubs for roughly the 20 to 40 age group, in several cities. Some chapters run the same group under another name, so it is worth asking locally rather than searching only for that one
Being the only person you know with one is the hardest part for most people this age, and it is the part a peer group fixes fastest.
Being in your twenties with one
If you are planning a pregnancy, start before you conceive — your gastroenterologist or surgeon, and an NSWOC. If you are already pregnant, tell your obstetric team about your ostomy at the first appointment and ask for an NSWOC to be involved early rather than when something goes wrong.

If your ostomy is because of IBD, the biggest thing you can influence is where your disease sits when you conceive. Going in while it is quiet is associated with outcomes close to anyone else’s, and conceiving during a flare makes preterm birth and low birth weight more likely

Start that conversation with your gastroenterologist before you start trying to conceive, rather than after. Some medication decisions take months to settle, and stopping treatment on your own is the thing most likely to go wrong

Getting pregnant may take longer if you have had pelvic surgery. Pouch surgery in particular is linked to reduced fertility — people with a pelvic pouch are around three times more likely to use IVF — though once they do, their chance of a live birth is the same as anyone else’s. Worth raising early, so that a slow start does not read as an answer

People with ostomies do have healthy pregnancies, and a stoma is not a reason not to. It does mean being followed more closely than usual: stoma problems in pregnancy are common rather than rare — blockage and a drop in output are the ones that come up most, and prolapse and parastomal hernia are also reported — and preterm birth is somewhat more likely. Almost all of it is manageable when your team knows to watch for it
Your abdomen changes shape substantially, so the stoma does too — expect to re-measure often and to change products more than once along the way

Settle one thing in advance: what counts as an emergency. Blockage is the most common stoma problem in pregnancy, so ask your surgeon or NSWOC now what should make you phone or come in. Get your own threshold and your own number before you need them
Most of what is known here comes from bowel stomas, so if you have a urostomy or ileal conduit, ask your urologist what is different for you.

How you deliver is a discussion between you, your obstetric team, your surgical team, and — if your ostomy is because of IBD — your gastroenterologist. Having a stoma does not decide it on its own, but some histories do push toward a planned caesarean, and in practice caesarean rates in people with a stoma run well above average. Ask early which of that applies to you

If you have an ileal pouch or a continent diversion, say so explicitly. A pouch is not a stoma, and guidelines lean toward a planned caesarean after pouch surgery to protect the sphincter and the pouch’s long-term function. The evidence behind that is not strong and teams do disagree, which is exactly why it belongs in a conversation months ahead rather than one in labour
The stoma usually settles back toward its pre-pregnancy size over the following weeks, so there is another round of re-measuring and probably another product change on the far side
Ask about lifting before you are home with a toddler to pick up. Parastomal hernia is the risk being managed, and the advice is specific to your surgery rather than general
Medication while breastfeeding is a gastroenterologist question if your ostomy is because of IBD. Stopping treatment unilaterally is the common mistake, and it is a phone call to avoid it
Dexterity and eyesight. Moldable barriers you shape with your fingers instead of cutting, larger tabs and simpler closures all exist for exactly this. Pre-cut works if your stoma is round and its size has settled; one-piece has fewer steps, while two-piece can be easier to line up by feel. There is no single right answer, so ask an NSWOC to trial a few with you rather than struggling with what you have

Skin gets thinner and tears more easily with age, and it usually shows up on removal — peel low and slow, pressing the skin away from the barrier rather than pulling the barrier off. Fit still matters just as much, because a barrier that leaks puts output onto skin that is slower to recover. Worth having an NSWOC watch you do a full change

Managing several conditions at once means more medication, and how much of a pill you absorb depends on your ostomy: with an ileostomy, extended-release and enteric-coated forms can pass through before they have finished working, while a colostomy is closer to normal. Ask a pharmacist to go through the whole list, including anything you buy over the counter

Home care and community nursing can help with changes — ask your care team what your province provides rather than assuming there is nothing. Most provinces also fund a pharmacist medication review, and in some, including Ontario, a pharmacist can come to you
If someone helps you, have them taught by an NSWOC directly — doing a change themselves with the nurse there, not just watching one. Book again if your stoma, your skin, or your products change

If a move to a retirement residence or long-term care is coming, raise the ostomy before the move rather than after. Staff frequently have no ostomy experience, and the route your supplies arrive by usually changes with the address
Several provincial programs cover more for seniors, and some are seniors-only — see Funding & Coverage.
Later life, and managing more than one thing
Ask what kind of help is wanted before offering it. Plenty of people want company and logistics, not hands-on care, and being asked is better than being managed
If you are doing hands-on care, ask an NSWOC to teach you directly — secondhand instructions are how skin problems start
Caring for someone is tiring in a way people underestimate. Most support groups welcome family and partners, and that is not an imposition on the group
If you are the one helping
Ostomy Canada’s Visitor Program puts you in touch with a trained peer visitor who has one themselves. It is support in its own right, not only a way to rehearse a difficult conversation, and it is free

A local chapter or peer support group is the other standing door, and several run online rather than only in person — worth knowing if you are rural, newly post-operative, or not ready to walk into a room. Listings do go stale, so if the one near you looks dead, Ostomy Canada’s national line is 1-888-969-9698

Low mood and anxiety are common after ostomy surgery, and they tend to rise in the months afterwards rather than settle. If it is not lifting, that is a reason to say so to your family doctor or surgical team — there is no ostomy-specific counselling service in Canada, so the route runs through your usual primary care and your province’s mental health services
Nothing here is a substitute for urgent help. If you are thinking about harming yourself, call or text 9-8-8, Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline, any time.
Where to bring the weight of it
chapters.this-might-be-you.categoriesInt: Most ostomy information is written for an average adult who does not exist. These are the situations where the differences are big enough to matter, and where the right move is usually a specific referral rather than a longer article.
The general advice is not wrong, it is just not enough
chapters.this-might-be-you.closing.body: The four situations here are the ones where general advice runs out fastest. Knowing that, and knowing who to ask, is genuinely most of the work.
chapters.this-might-be-you.closing.headi: Most of this is a conversation, not an article
chapters.this-might-be-you.focus: Children and the people raising them, young adults, pregnancy and parenthood, and older adults — what changes for each, and who to ask rather than guess.
chapters.this-might-be-you.governance.di: This is general information, not medical advice. Care for children, during pregnancy, and for people managing several conditions differs in ways this page does not attempt to cover — it is here to tell you what changes and who to ask. Speak to an NSWOC and the treating team rather than relying on general ostomy guidance, including ours.
chapters.this-might-be-you.heroBody: What is genuinely different if you are a child’s parent, in your twenties, thinking about pregnancy, or managing this alongside other things in later life.
chapters.this-might-be-you.pharmacist.bo: An Ontario pharmacist can help with what products exist in smaller sizes, what is easier to handle, and how a medication list looks alongside an ostomy — during business hours until 5 p.m. Eastern. Anything about a child, a pregnancy, or a change in someone’s ability to manage belongs with an NSWOC or the treating team.
chapters.this-might-be-you.pharmacist.he: Product and restock questions, whoever you are
Your child’s hospital team first — they hold the referral to a nurse who works in pediatrics. Ask about Youth Camp early; funding exists and places are limited.
Before you conceive if you can: your gastroenterologist or surgeon, then your obstetric team from the first appointment, with an NSWOC involved early rather than reactively.
Your NSWOC for fit as dexterity changes, a pharmacist for a full medication review, and your province’s home care program.
The referral that fits each one
chapters.this-might-be-you.title: This Might Be You
chapters.this-might-be-you.vibe: Specific, and quick to refer — short on advice, clear on who actually knows.
funding.governance.disclaimer: This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for assessment by your NSWOC, surgeon, or physician. Fit, skin, and product choices depend on your body and your surgery — talk to your care team before changing anything. Funding amounts and eligibility rules change every year — always confirm on the official government page before planning around a number.
funding.models.categorical.blurb: There is no general program. Coverage runs through specific routes — seniors, social assistance, or a named condition — so the question is which category you fall into.
funding.models.categorical.label: Only if you qualify
funding.models.cost-share.blurb: The program covers a share and you pay the rest, often up to an annual maximum. Low income usually reduces or removes your share.
funding.models.cost-share.label: A percentage cost-share
funding.models.flat-grant.blurb: A set amount arrives each year and you buy your own supplies. Anything above the grant is yours to cover — and may be claimable as a medical expense at tax time.
funding.models.flat-grant.label: A flat grant, paid to you
funding.models.none.blurb: Nothing covers ostomy supplies directly here. Federal routes and tax credits may still help.
funding.models.none.label: No ostomy-specific program
funding.models.supplies-in-kind.blurb: The program sends the supplies rather than reimbursing you, so you are registered rather than applying — and you do not buy them at retail.
funding.models.supplies-in-kind.label: Supplies issued to you
funding.programs.AB.amount: You pay 25% of the cost, up to a maximum of $500 per family per benefit year — after which AADL covers 100% for the rest of the year. The $500 is a ceiling on what you pay, not an amount you receive.
funding.programs.AB.deadlines: The benefit year runs 1 July to 30 June.
funding.programs.AB.gatekeeper: An AADL-approved authoriser — for ostomy products this is a registered nurse, and in practice usually an NSWOC.
funding.programs.AB.howToApply: An AADL-approved authoriser assesses you and authorises the products; an approved vendor then bills AADL directly and charges you your share at the point of sale.
funding.programs.AB.name: Alberta
funding.programs.AB.notes: Low-income Albertans and income-assistance recipients pay nothing at all. If you are excluded because another plan covers you fully — Veterans Affairs, NIHB, or WCB — that other plan is the route.
funding.programs.BC.amount: After an income-based family deductible, PharmaCare pays 70% of eligible costs — 75% if a family member was born before 1940 — then 100% once you reach the family maximum.
funding.programs.BC.deadlines: Return the mailed consent form within 30 days or registration does not complete. Deductibles run on the calendar year.
funding.programs.BC.gatekeeper: Nobody clinical — registration and CRA income verification are the gate. The practical gatekeeper is a provider who can bill under a listed product code.
funding.programs.BC.howToApply: There is no ostomy application. The step that matters is registering for Fair PharmaCare, which sets your deductible. Register at gov.bc.ca or on 1-800-663-7100, then coverage applies automatically at the till through an authorised provider.
funding.programs.BC.name: British Columbia
funding.programs.BC.notes: If you do not register for Fair PharmaCare you are assigned a $10,000 deductible by default, which means paying for everything yourself. Registering is the single highest-value thing a BC reader can do. Note that skin barriers, protectants, deodorants and cleansers are not covered — people routinely assume they are.
funding.programs.MB.deadlines: Order at least two weeks ahead. You can request up to three months of supplies at a time.
funding.programs.MB.gatekeeper: An NSWOC, who sets your supply list. Any change to that list also needs NSWOC approval.
funding.programs.MB.howToApply: You are registered by an NSWOC after surgery rather than applying yourself. The program then covers basic supplies in full and sends them to you — there is nothing to pay and nothing to claim back.
funding.programs.MB.name: Manitoba
funding.programs.MB.notes: There is no dollar figure here, and that is correct rather than missing — limits are set per product in quantities, not in money. Any number you find quoted for Manitoba is not a current benefit rate.
funding.programs.NB.gatekeeper: Your Social Development health card is the gate — it must show the right supplementary or ostomy eligibility code.
funding.programs.NB.howToApply: There is no general ostomy program in New Brunswick. If you are a Social Development client with a qualifying health card, eligible supplies cost you nothing and the program pays pharmacies and suppliers directly. If you are not, this route is closed and the federal and tax options below are where to look.
funding.programs.NB.name: New Brunswick
funding.programs.NB.notes: Coverage is capped by monthly quantities per product rather than by dollars — for example a set number of wafers and pouches each month.
funding.programs.NL.amount: Reimburses 75% of the retail cost of eligible items — but only for 65Plus Plan cardholders, meaning seniors receiving both Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
funding.programs.NL.gatekeeper: No separate assessor — a prescription and your 65Plus card are what is needed.
funding.programs.NL.howToApply: Enrolment happens automatically through your OAS and GIS status. You buy the supplies, keep the original prescription receipts, and claim the 75% back.
funding.programs.NL.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
funding.programs.NL.notes: If you are under 65, or not receiving GIS, the official page does not name you as eligible for this subsidy. Check the other NLPDP plans and the federal routes below.
funding.programs.NS.amount: Ostomy products are a listed Pharmacare benefit, so what you pay depends on which plan you are in rather than on an ostomy-specific rate.
funding.programs.NS.deadlines: Reimbursement claims must be submitted within six months of the prescription being dispensed — the most commonly missed deadline in the province.
funding.programs.NS.gatekeeper: A physician or nurse practitioner prescribes. An NSWOC is not a gatekeeper here. Plan enrolment is the real step.
funding.programs.NS.howToApply: Ostomy products are dispensed as prescriptions through a Nova Scotia pharmacy, so the route is a prescriber plus enrolment in a Pharmacare plan. Family Pharmacare is open to any resident without other drug coverage — worth knowing, because Nova Scotia is often described as having nothing for the general public, and that is not right.
funding.programs.NS.name: Nova Scotia
funding.programs.NS.notes: If you are in active cancer treatment with a combined family income of $35,000 or less, the Boarding, Transportation and Ostomy program reimburses actual supply costs on top. Seniors and Income Assistance clients have their own cost-sharing rules.
funding.programs.NT.amount: Seniors 60+ and lower-income bands pay nothing. Higher bands pay 25% of the cost up to a yearly family maximum of $500 to $1,500 depending on income band, after which the plan pays everything. There is no deductible on medical supplies.
funding.programs.NT.deadlines: Bands and maximums reset on 1 September.
funding.programs.NT.gatekeeper: Program registration plus a prescription from a recognised health care prescriber.
funding.programs.NT.howToApply: Register under the Extended Health Benefits policy, which involves an income assessment — unless you are 60 or over, in which case you are enrolled on age. A prescriber then orders the supplies.
funding.programs.NT.name: Northwest Territories
funding.programs.NT.notes: Ostomy supplies are covered under general medical supplies rather than a named ostomy benefit. First Nations and Inuit residents go through NIHB instead.
funding.programs.NU.gatekeeper: A prescription is required either way.
funding.programs.NU.howToApply: There is no ostomy-specific program. If you qualify under specified conditions or seniors coverage, prescribed medical supplies are covered including fitting and shipping — which matters a great deal in Nunavut. Most Nunavummiut are Inuit and are covered federally through NIHB instead.
funding.programs.NU.name: Nunavut
funding.programs.NU.notes: Nunavut publishes no amount, cap, or per-item rate for supplies, and no list we could confirm of which conditions qualify. Call Extended Health Benefits on 867-645-8029 to ask whether your diagnosis is on the list rather than assuming either way.
funding.programs.ON.amount: You receive $975 per ostomy per year, paid in two instalments. That rises to $1,300 if you live in a long-term care home or receive social assistance.
funding.programs.ON.deadlines: Renew every two years; ADP sends paperwork about three months before expiry. Reviews take up to eight weeks, with the first payment within 30 days of approval.
funding.programs.ON.gatekeeper: A physician or nurse practitioner — an NSWOC signature is not required here, which differs from several other provinces.
funding.programs.ON.howToApply: A physician or nurse practitioner examines you and confirms the ostomy, you both complete form 014-1945-67, and it goes to the Assistive Devices Program. The money is paid to you, not to a vendor, so you can buy supplies wherever you like.
funding.programs.ON.name: Ontario
funding.programs.ON.notes: A temporary ostomy only qualifies if it is needed for longer than six months. If you receive ODSP, the Mandatory Special Necessities benefit can cover costs above the grant — but only once the ADP grant is used up.
funding.programs.PE.amount: Reimburses 60% to 100% of what you spend depending on household income, up to $2,400 per full program year.
funding.programs.PE.deadlines: The program year runs 1 July to 30 June and you must re-apply before it expires or coverage stops. Old invoices are not accepted, so submit regularly rather than saving them up.
funding.programs.PE.gatekeeper: A health care professional — the program does not specifically require an NSWOC.
funding.programs.PE.howToApply: A health care professional submits the Health Care Provider Registration Form for you. After that it is income-tested rather than clinical.
funding.programs.PE.name: Prince Edward Island
funding.programs.PE.notes: Joining part-way through the year pro-rates the maximum.
funding.programs.QC.amount: An annual lump sum of $1,510 for a permanent ostomy, or $1,007 for a temporary one. Paid per ostomy, so two stomas means two allocations.
funding.programs.QC.deadlines: Amounts are indexed every 1 January. Temporary-ostomy payments are split — half when the application is accepted, then every six months until the stoma is closed.
funding.programs.QC.gatekeeper: No clinical sign-off is needed to submit — you apply directly.
funding.programs.QC.howToApply: You apply to RAMQ yourself. The only conditions are being insured under the Québec Health Insurance Plan and having had a colostomy, ileostomy or urostomy.
funding.programs.QC.name: Quebec
funding.programs.QC.notes: If you hold a claim slip through social assistance you are reimbursed at actual cost instead of the lump sum. There is also a voluntary agreement that pays your supplier directly and ends the lump-sum payments — useful for some people, but it is a one-way switch worth understanding first.
funding.programs.SK.amount: The province pays 50% of eligible supplies within quantity limits, and you pay the other half. There is no annual dollar cap.
funding.programs.SK.gatekeeper: An ET/NSWOC nurse at a provincial stoma clinic. Registration comes before coverage.
funding.programs.SK.howToApply: Referral from an ET/NSWOC nurse at a Saskatchewan stoma clinic. This is the only route in — a prescription from your family doctor will not register you, and there is no way to apply for yourself.
funding.programs.SK.name: Saskatchewan
funding.programs.SK.notes: Some people get supplies at no charge rather than at 50% — Paraplegia Program registrants, and holders of Supplementary Health Benefits through SAID, SIS or SEI. Worth asking about before assuming you pay half.
funding.programs.YT.deadlines: Apply before you buy. Purchases made outside Yukon without prior approval must be claimed within one year.
funding.programs.YT.gatekeeper: A physician or community health nurse. Note that having an ostomy is not by itself a qualifying condition — coverage runs through a closed list of chronic diseases, and several common causes of ostomy are not on it. Confirm your specific diagnosis before assuming you are covered.
funding.programs.YT.howToApply: Your physician — or a community health nurse where there is no resident doctor — applies on your behalf, and pre-approval before you buy is expected. If you are 65 or over you are covered instead through Seniors Pharmacare, enrolled automatically.
funding.programs.YT.name: Yukon
funding.programs.YT.notes: Yukon publishes no ostomy figure and no deductible amount on its own pages. Numbers circulate elsewhere; we are not repeating them, because we could not confirm them. Call the program to get your own numbers before planning around them.
ui.chapter.crisis.body: Nothing here is a substitute for urgent help. If you are thinking about harming yourself, call or text 9-8-8, Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline, any time.
ui.chapter.productsNote: Liivv sells these. They are here because this section is about equipment — nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy from us.
ui.chapter.resourcesIntro: These are run by patient organizations, specialist nurses, and government programs — not by Liivv. We link out because they do this better than a shop could.
ui.chapter.takeIn.notesHint: The printed list has space to write down answers.
ui.checker.caveat: This is a starting point, not a decision. Programs change their amounts and rules every year — always confirm on the official page before you plan around a number, and your NSWOC can often tell you what actually gets approved locally.

ui.discovery.heading: Ostomy is one of the things we support
ui.discovery.hubBody: Eleven areas of care, with more on the way.
ui.discovery.lead: If something else is part of your everyday — yours or someone you care for — there is a chapter for that too.
ui.fundingPage.arrive1: Find an NSWOC early — in several provinces you cannot register at all without one.
ui.fundingPage.arrive2: Check the new province’s model above. If you move from a grant province to a supplies-in-kind one, you stop buying at retail entirely.
ui.fundingPage.arrive3: Expect a waiting period, and budget for it.
ui.fundingPage.before1: Claim anything outstanding — most programs will not pay across a move.
ui.fundingPage.before2: Ask your NSWOC for a written summary of your current setup, sizes, and products. It shortens registration at the other end considerably.
ui.fundingPage.before3: Stock up enough to cover the gap while new coverage is approved.
ui.fundingPage.closingBody: If the numbers are not working, that is worth saying out loud to your care team. There are usually more routes than people realise.
ui.fundingPage.closingHeading: Money should not be the reason you ration supplies
ui.fundingPage.dtcNote: The most valuable and most misunderstood item on this page — and the one people most often get refused.
ui.fundingPage.dtcPoint1: Having an ostomy does not qualify you on its own. This is the part almost every summary gets wrong. A well-managed routine is frequently refused, and the CRA’s own guidance says so.
ui.fundingPage.dtcPoint2: The test: you are unable to manage bowel or bladder function, or it takes you roughly three times longer than someone of similar age without the impairment, at least 90% of the time, for a continuous 12 months — assessed with your appliances and routine already in place.
ui.fundingPage.dtcPoint3: So what gets approved is complications and time burden, not the stoma itself. Leaks, skin breakdown, repeated changes, night-time management, time lost from work — that is what belongs on the form.
ui.fundingPage.dtcPoint4: Apply through the eliminating category — bowel or bladder function — not life-sustaining therapy. Only a medical doctor or nurse practitioner can certify it. Your NSWOC can help you describe your routine accurately, but cannot sign the form.
ui.fundingPage.dtcPoint5: It is still worth applying: approval can be backdated up to ten years, and it unlocks the RDSP and the Canada Disability Benefit. A refusal costs you those too, which is why the wording matters so much.
ui.fundingPage.dtcPoint6: If you are refused, the medical expense claim below needs no approval at all.
ui.fundingPage.expensesHeading: Medical expenses on your tax return
ui.fundingPage.expensesPoint1: Whatever your province does not cover may be claimable. Several provinces say so explicitly on their own program pages.
ui.fundingPage.expensesPoint2: Keep receipts, including shipping where it is not covered.
ui.fundingPage.federalHeading: Help that does not depend on where you live
ui.fundingPage.focus: Provincial and territorial coverage, federal programs, the Disability Tax Credit, and what to do when the funding runs out before the year does.
ui.fundingPage.lead: There is no national ostomy program in Canada. The amount, the model, and who signs off all change at the provincial border — so the first useful thing to know is which system you are in.
ui.fundingPage.metaDescription: What each province and territory pays toward ostomy supplies, how to apply, who has to sign off, and the federal tax credits worth claiming. Every figure links to its official source.
ui.fundingPage.metaTitle: Ostomy funding in Canada — what your province covers | Liivv
ui.fundingPage.modelsIntro: Almost every misunderstanding about ostomy funding comes from assuming your province works like a different one. There are really only four models.
ui.fundingPage.movingIntro: Nobody writes this down, and it catches people out. Moving resets your coverage entirely — different model, different amount, different forms, and often a different person who has to sign them.
ui.fundingPage.nihbPoint1: For registered First Nations and recognized Inuit, NIHB covers approved ostomy items subject to quantity limits and prior approval. Recognized providers bill NIHB directly, so there is no upfront cost to you.
ui.fundingPage.nihbPoint2: This replaces the provincial route rather than topping it up — so start here rather than applying to your province first.
ui.fundingPage.nihbPoint3: There is an exception process for quantities or items outside the standard list. High output is a common and legitimate reason to use it.
ui.fundingPage.ranOut1Body: Often the fastest win is not more money but a better fit — fewer changes, longer wear time, less waste. An NSWOC can also tell you what actually gets approved in your region.
ui.fundingPage.ranOut2Body: Hollister, Coloplast, and Convatec all run free support lines with samples and nurse access, regardless of where you buy. They will also help you navigate coverage.
ui.fundingPage.ranOut3Body: Provincial disability and social assistance programs sometimes top up ostomy coverage above the standard grant. This is worth asking about directly.
ui.fundingPage.ranOut3Heading: Check social assistance and disability routes
ui.fundingPage.ranOut4Body: Ostomy Canada chapters know the local landscape, and some hold donated supplies. Treat second-hand product carefully — check the expiry date, that the inner packaging is unopened, that the size matches what you use, and ask how it was stored.
ui.fundingPage.ranOutHeading: The funding ran out before the year did

ui.help.groupBody: Chapters and peer support across the country, searchable by distance from where you live. They also train peer visitors who have an ostomy themselves.
ui.help.groupTitle: Find a support group near you
ui.help.heading: Two people worth finding
ui.help.lead: Most of what helps most is not a product. These are free, they are not run by us, and they are the two contacts people most often wish they had found sooner.
ui.help.nswocBody: The nurse specialists for stoma care in Canada. Many hospitals have one, and many see outpatients for life — fit, skin, and anything about the stoma itself belongs with them.
ui.help.talkBody: Ontario pharmacist chat for product and restock questions during business hours. Not a substitute for your NSWOC on anything clinical.
ui.results.deadlinesTitle: Dates that quietly cost people money
ui.results.dtcBody: Having an ostomy does not qualify you on its own, and a well-managed routine is often refused. The test is whether you are unable to manage bowel or bladder function, or it takes about three times longer than it would for someone of similar age without the impairment, at least 90% of the time, for a continuous 12 months — judged even with your appliances and routine in place. That means complications, leaks and time burden are what the form has to show. Only a medical doctor or nurse practitioner can certify it.
ui.results.dtcTitle: The Disability Tax Credit — worth applying for, but read the test first
ui.results.expensesBody: This one has no gate. Ostomy pads and supplies are listed eligible medical expenses, so whatever your province does not cover may be claimable on your return whether or not you have the Disability Tax Credit. Keep every receipt, including shipping where it is not covered.
ui.results.expensesTitle: Claim what you paid out of pocket — no approval needed
ui.results.lastResortBody: This territory is a payer of last resort, which means private or employer insurance has to be exhausted before the territorial program pays anything. Submit to your insurer first and keep the statement — you will need it.
ui.results.lastResortTitle: Your workplace plan gets billed first
ui.results.nihbBody: For registered First Nations and recognized Inuit, NIHB covers approved ostomy items subject to quantity limits and prior approval, and recognized providers bill NIHB directly so you do not pay upfront. This replaces the provincial route rather than topping it up. Ask about the exception process if you need more than the standard quantity — high output is a common reason.
ui.results.permanenceTitle: Temporary ostomies are treated differently here
ui.results.provisionalBody: You told us about age and whether your ostomy is permanent. Both genuinely change what some provinces fund, but we have not yet verified those rules against each government page — so we are not guessing. Check the official link above for your own situation, and ask the program directly.
